prompt.context: Our client is a pharmaceutical company that has developed a remedy for female balding. The drug has cleared a lengthy and delayed testing process. The drug will be off patent in five years. Before initiating drug production, the client wants us to determine whether the drug will be profitable and whether or not to go ahead with production.
prompt.question: Should the client proceed with production of this drug? Is the drug profitable? After your profitability analysis, you will also be asked to recommend a market entry strategy based on clinical trial results for two formulations.

clarifying_info.q: Are there competing products in the market?
clarifying_info.a: One comparable substitute currently exists that will divide market share equally with client once the client's drug is in the market. Post-patent expiry, the client's share will shrink to 20% of share pre-patent expiry.

clarifying_info.q: What is the price of the product?
clarifying_info.a: Assume the price is comparable to the substitute at $2,000 per treatment, and that one treatment is needed per year.

clarifying_info.q: What age range is affected by female balding?
clarifying_info.a: Average woman starts balding at age 40. Between ages 30-40 the drug has some preventative benefits. Starting at age 60, even the most effective drugs cannot remedy female balding.

clarifying_info.q: Does health insurance cover the product?
clarifying_info.a: Payment for the product is not covered by most health insurance plans.

clarifying_info.q: What costs has the client incurred so far?
clarifying_info.a: $8B was spent on testing (note: sunk cost). Annual operating costs going forward: Production $1B/year, Marketing and sales $2.5B/year, Distribution $800M/year.

clarifying_info.q: Do the two products have a comparative advantage over each other?
clarifying_info.a: Assume our drug and the current comparable substitute have no comparative advantage over the other; both will charge the same price and split the market equally.

exhibits.title: Customer Survey
exhibits.shows: A bar chart titled 'Importance of Product Characteristic by Age Cohort' showing ratings (scale 0-5) of three characteristics — Effectiveness, Convenience/Ease of Use, and Cost — broken out for three age groups: 30-40, 40-50, and 50-60.
exhibits.data: Rating scale 0-5; three characteristics: Effectiveness, Convenience/Ease of Use, Cost; three age cohorts: 30-40, 40-50, 50-60

framework: Define the profitability question: Revenue – Costs > 0 over the patent period and post-patent
Size the market: estimate addressable U.S. female population by age bracket, apply interest rates, then affordability filter
Calculate revenue: target population × client market share × price per treatment
Calculate costs: identify sunk vs. ongoing costs; sum annual operating costs
Go/No-Go recommendation: compare annual profit pre- and post-patent expiry
Bonus: launch strategy for two formulations based on customer segment preferences

questions.prompt: Question 1: Size the market and determine whether the drug will be profitable.
questions.guidance: Candidate should work through a demand-side market sizing (population by age bracket, interest rate, affordability filter), then apply market share and price to get revenue, then compare to ongoing costs. Sunk cost ($8B testing) should be excluded. Key insight: drug is profitable pre-patent expiry but marginally so or unprofitable post-expiry.

math.setup: U.S. population = 320M; 50% female = 160M; divide into 10-year brackets of 20M each. Apply interest rates by bracket, then affordability filter. Client gets 50% of addressable market pre-patent, 20% of that post-patent.
steps: Step 1 – Interested population by age bracket (revised rates): Age 30-40: 20M × 20% = 4M; Age 40-50: 20M × 30% = 6M; Age 50-60: 20M × 30% = 6M; Total interested = 16M

Step 2 – Affordability filter on 16M interested: Low income (20% = 3.2M) × 0% able = 0; Middle income (60% = 9.6M) × 30% able = 2.88M ≈ 3M; Upper income (20% = 3.2M) × 100% able = 3.2M ≈ 3M; Total able to pay = ~6M
Step 5 – Annual costs (ongoing only, exclude sunk $8B): Production $1B + Marketing $2.5B + Distribution $0.8B = $4.3B
Step 7 – Revenue post-patent: client share shrinks to 20% of pre-patent share → 3M × 20% = 0.6M patients × $2,000 = $1.2B
Step 8 – Annual profit post-patent: $1.2B – $4.3B = –$3.1B (unprofitable at current cost structure)
math.answer: Drug generates ~$1.7B annual profit pre-patent expiry; post-patent the drug is unprofitable at current costs (~–$3.1B/year). Go/No-Go: proceed for the 5-year patent window; reassess cost structure before patent expiry.

questions.prompt: Question 2: Based on clinical trial results and the customer survey (Exhibit 1), recommend which formulation(s) the client should launch and outline a market entry strategy.
questions.guidance: Candidate should map the two formulations to customer segments using the exhibit. Formulation 1 (once-daily, lower price, less effective) suits cost- and convenience-focused older women (40-60). Formulation 2 (twice-daily, higher price, most effective) suits effectiveness-focused younger women (30-40). Candidate should weigh segment size vs. lifetime value and give a clear single recommendation with rationale, then note risks.

math.setup: No required calculation; qualitative exhibit interpretation.
steps: Formulation 1 maps to age 40-60 cohorts: high importance on Cost and Convenience/Ease of Use
Formulation 2 maps to age 30-40 cohort: high importance on Effectiveness
Older cohort (40-60) = larger potential market but shorter lifetime value
Younger cohort (30-40) = smaller market but longer lifetime value (preventive use)
math.answer: Recommend launching Formulation 1 (once-daily, lower price) targeting women aged 40-60, as this is the primary and larger market segment. Do not launch both simultaneously to avoid brand confusion and diluted marketing resources.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the risks to profitability and the launch strategy that the client should consider?

categories.name: Competitive risks
ideas: Competitor lowers price in response to entry, eroding client's price parity assumption
Competitor's patent expires before client's, triggering further share loss
New entrants attracted by the unmet need (only 2 products in market)

categories.name: Market sizing risks
ideas: Marketing costs may be insufficient to educate consumers about product existence
Interest and affordability assumptions may be off — actual addressable market could be smaller
Insurance coverage could expand or contract, shifting affordability dynamics

categories.name: Product/formulation risks
ideas: Launching only Formulation 1 cedes the younger, higher-willingness-to-pay segment to competitors
Price sensitivity differs significantly between 40-50 and 50-60 cohorts
Branding a once-daily convenience product may limit premium pricing later

categories.name: Cost structure risks
ideas: Marketing and distribution costs may not scale down post-patent, making the business unviable
Expenses may vary over the product lifecycle in ways not captured in flat annual estimates

recommendation: Proceed with drug production for the five-year patent window; the drug generates approximately $1.7B annual profit pre-patent expiry under the stated assumptions
For launch, produce Formulation 1 (once-daily, lower price) and target women aged 40-60 with a branding strategy focused on once-a-day convenience
risks: Post-patent profitability is negative at current cost structure — continued production after year 5 requires significant cost reduction or market expansion
Launching only Formulation 1 may cede younger, higher-value customers to a competitor willing to offer a more effective product
Competitor response (price cut or new formulation) could compress margins during the patent period
next_steps: Determine whether costs (especially marketing and distribution) can be reduced post-patent to make continued production viable
Explore international markets where U.S. testing approval is recognized as an incremental revenue opportunity
Evaluate a staged launch: establish brand with Formulation 1, then introduce Formulation 2 as a premium 'extra-strength' alternative post-launch
Consider adjacent segments (men, hair regrowth) to broaden the revenue base before patent expiry
